<header class="c-pagehead">
  <div class="c-wrap">
    <p class="c-eyebrow">Division · Molecular</p>
    <h1>Computational Biology</h1>
    <p>
      High-throughput biological data, read for mechanism. We work mainly in
      oncogenomics, looking for the molecular events that separate one tumour from
      another and the biomarkers that make that difference actionable.
    </p>
  </div>
</header>

<section class="c-slab c-slab--paper">
  <div class="c-wrap">
    <div class="c-split">
      <div class="c-prose">

        <h2>Multi-omics integration in cancer</h2>
        <p>
          Genomics, transcriptomics, epigenomics, proteomics and metabolomics each
          describe one layer of a tumour. Integrated, they describe a system. We
          synthesise multi-dimensional data from international consortia — TCGA,
          GEO, ICGC — to characterise tumour heterogeneity and identify clinically
          actionable targets.
        </p>

        <h2>Bulk RNA sequencing</h2>
        <p>
          Bulk RNA-seq gives a high-resolution view of the transcriptome across a
          sample. We use it for differential expression, isoform discovery, gene
          fusion detection and alternative splicing analysis across pathological
          states.
        </p>

        <h2>Single-cell transcriptomics</h2>
        <p>
          scRNA-seq resolves expression to the individual cell, which is where the
          interesting heterogeneity usually lives. Our work here concerns the
          tumour microenvironment, rare cell populations, and the cell-state
          trajectories that accompany progression and immune response.
        </p>

        <h2>Structural &amp; molecular modelling</h2>
        <p>
          Where a target emerges from the omics work, we follow it structurally —
          binding-site characterisation, docking and stability assessment — to
          judge whether it is tractable.
        </p>

        <h2>Selected outputs</h2>
        <p>
          <a href="../../publications.html">Pan-cancer analysis reveals immunological and prognostic significance of CCT5 in human tumors</a>,
          <em>Cancer Bioinformatics</em>, 2025.
        </p>
